content:
Hi everyone! I've been profiling where time goes when LLM provers run Lean, and (n)linarith turned out to be ~half the marginal compute on a miniF2F workload. I built a package around two ideas and I'd love scrutiny on both:

  1. a Rust reimplementation of linarith's simplex certificate search behind Mathlib's pluggable CertificateOracle. The interface has always been meant for this — Lewis & Wu demonstrated a Mathematica-backed oracle in the Lean 3 era (arXiv:2101.07758, ~20 lines!); farkas is, to my knowledge, the first local, exact, production-oriented oracle behind the Lean 4 interface — and the first where the oracle is the fast part. And
  2. a "probe-then-restrict" fast path: parse hypotheses numerically (no proof terms), ask the oracle which hypotheses matter (median: 1), then run stock linarith only [...] on just those.

Measured on 438 machine-generated miniF2F proofs, live-REPL regime: (n)linarith time −63%, marginal end-to-end −31%, 96% of invocations take the fast path. Full setup, definitions and threats to validity: docs/evaluation.md. Reproduce with one command, or measure your own workload: docs/corpus.md.

On trust: the fast path only selects hypotheses — every proof is still built by stock linarith and checked by the kernel; a wrong oracle answer can cause a tactic failure, never a wrong proof. A missing daemon degrades to stock silently. CI runs Mathlib's own linarith tests stock-vs-fast and requires byte-identical diagnostics.

Honest limitations: gains are bounded by linarith's share of your workload; the numbers come from one corpus family; ℝ≥0 and ≠ goals always take the fallback; and yes — the shadow-elaborator activation is a maintenance liability I'd like to remove by upstreaming a set_option linarith.oracle hook (separate thread coming; the interface was clearly designed for this).

Also possibly useful independently: docs/certificate-lp-spec.md documents the exact semantics of linarith's oracle contract, mechanically validated against 4,548 certificates. And for the grind question: measured relationship in docs/grind.md — grind's current gap on this workload is almost entirely nlinarith.

github.com/lucifer1004/farkas — feedback very welcome, especially breakage reports.

@Gabriel Wu, thanks, this is interesting. (Please do remember to not post text here as your own words that has been written by an LLM, even just for translation purposes. Your text above has lots of tells!)

Could you explain how (1) and (2) separately affect the performance improvements you see?

What is the corpus? "machine-generated" can mean many things, and we know that older LLMs proofs really liked linarith and nlinarith, and used them too much, so there's some caution warranted here about whether you're targeting a historical artefact.

(Separately, unfortunately for at least two weeks I won't have time to look at this, note there is also my leanprover/lp, which is about 2x the speed of linarith, but for somewhat orthogonal reasons. That's a standalone package that doesn't need mathlib. It also has no nlinarith type functionality. I've been meaning to see if any of the speed-up there is translatable to the mathlib linarith. I'm actually a little surprised you see any improvement from a Rust backend, as on the Mathlib linarith workload the oracle is really not the limiting factor, but this may be a feature of the LLM generated workload.)

Thanks Kim! Sorry for violating the community rules. I meant to be more accurate via help from LLM.

The contribution of each part is shown in the table below:

configuration (n)linarith time marginal end-to-end
stock Mathlib 893 s 1,802 s
+ native oracle 655 s 1,567 s
+ probe-then-restrict fast path 328 s (−63%) 1,236 s (−31%)

For the oracle part, the gain mainly comes from the long tail (problems can have up to 13k nonzeros with coeffs up to 1e606). The median is actually small (4.18 ms only).

For the corpus part, I used DeepSeek-Prover-V2's published miniF2F solutions, which has 438 files and 2910 (n)linarith calls. But the conclusion is general enough. Hit rate is 82.5% on 14 linarith-dense Mathlib modules and 76.8% on MathlibTest/Tactic/Linarith, vs 96.2% on the tuning corpus.

For the lp part, I think our speedup mechanism can be complementary. lp replaces the procedure, while farkas keeps Mathlib's linarith and removes wasted preprocessing via selection.
